सार
Meerut News: रविवार को दिन निकलते ही तेज धूप के कारण मौसम गर्म हो गया। दोपहर को गर्मी का अहसास हो रहा है। वहीं शाम होने के साथ ही ठंडक बढ़ेगी। वहीं बदलते मौसम में लोगों को बीमारियों के प्रति भी सतर्क रहने की चेतावनी दी गई है।

विस्तार
पश्चिमी उत्तर प्रदेश में अक्तूबर के दूसरे पखवाड़े में भी गर्मी का असर बना हुआ है। दिन में तेज धूप के कारण लोगों को गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ रहा है, हालांकि रात के समय तापमान में गिरावट से कुछ राहत मिल रही है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, अगले दो से तीन दिनों तक मौसम में इसी तरह उतार-चढ़ाव बना रह सकता है।

दिन चढ़ने के साथ ही धूप तेज होने से गर्मी का असर बढ़ रहा है। दोपहर के समय धूप में निकलने वाले लोगों को परेशानी हो रही है। सुबह और शाम के समय मौसम सामान्य बना हुआ है। रात में तापमान में गिरावट आने से हल्की ठंडक का अहसास हो रहा है। मौसम के इस बदलाव के चलते दिन में गर्मी और रात में राहत का दौर जारी है। आगामी दिनों में भी आसमान साफ रहने और तेज धूप निकलने की स्थिति में दिन के तापमान में दो से तीन डिग्री तक बढ़ोतरी होने की संभावना है, जबकि रात का मौसम अपेक्षाकृत राहत भरा रह सकता है।

- कॉपी लिंक
कोटा संभाग में मौसम का मिजाज रोजाना बदल रहा है। तापमान में जारी उतार-चढ़ाव के बीच शनिवार को अधिकतम तापमान में 2 डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की गई थी, जिसके बाद रविवार सुबह से ही शहर में धूप खिली रही। धूप में आई तेजी के कारण दिन के समय शहरवासियों को हल्की उमस और गर्माहट का सामना करना पड़ा।
हालांकि, मौसम विभाग का अनुमान है कि दोपहर बाद या शाम तक आंशिक रूप से बादल छाने और तेज हवाएं चलने से तापमान में फिर गिरावट दर्ज की जा सकती है। कोटा में अधिकतम तापमान में 2 डिग्री की बढ़ोतरी के साथ यह 35.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया।
न्यूनतम तापमान में विशेष बदलाव नहीं हुआ और यह 23.6 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा। दो दिन पहले अधिकतम तापमान 37 डिग्री व न्यूनतम तापमान 25.1 डिग्री सेल्सियस था। वहीं शुक्रवार-शनिवार को 33 डिग्री तक हो गया था।
पश्चिमी विक्षोभ का दिख रहा असर मौसम विशेषज्ञों के अनुसार, प्रदेश के कई अन्य जिलों की तरह कोटा संभाग में भी पश्चिमी विक्षोभ और परिसंचरण तंत्र की सक्रियता का मिला-जुला असर बना हुआ है। राज्य के कई हिस्सों में मेघगर्जना के साथ हल्की से मध्यम बारिश दर्ज की गई है, जिससे संभाग में भी हवा की दिशा और नमी में लगातार बदलाव आ रहा है। शनिवार को जहां दिन में तेज धूप के बाद शाम को बादल छाए रहे और ठंडी हवाएं चलीं, वहीं रविवार को भी सुबह से तेज धूप के साथ बादलों की आवाजाही का सिलसिला देखने को मिला।
आगे कैसा रहेगा मौसम का हाल जयपुर मौसम केंद्र के अनुसार, कोटा संभाग में अगले 24 से 48 घंटों के दौरान कहीं-कहीं हल्की बूंदाबांदी या छिटपुट बारिश की संभावना से इंकार नहीं किया जा सकता। तेज हवाएं चलने के कारण दिन में धूप रहने के बावजूद रात के तापमान में धीरे-धीरे गिरावट आएगी, जिससे सुबह और देर रात में गुलाबी ठंड का अहसास बढ़ने लगेगा।

Pregnancy and childbirth have become a “new fault line in the global climate crisis” as extreme heat worsens, the head of the UN climate action body (UNFCCC) warned on Monday, calling for maternal and newborn health to be built into countries’ climate plans.
Every day more than 1 billion meals are left uneaten. From a food security perspective, this mountain of discarded food is problematic. But it creates other problems as well. As it decomposes in landfills, rotting food releases enough methane to make it one of the major drivers of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions.

Panaji: An upper-air cyclonic circulation over the southeast Arabian Sea has triggered cloudy conditions over Goa since Friday, bringing very heavy rainfall of 117.4mm to Dabolim in the 24 hours till Saturday morning, while a few other centres received moderate to light showers.
The rainfall brought relief after a dry post-monsoon season, with activity dipping in Sept, and slightly reduced the rainfall deficit.
“An extreme rainfall event over Dabolim station is quite unusual, which again shows the highly discrete nature of rainfall even within a small state like Goa,” said M R Ramesh Kumar, chief scientist (retired) and meteorologist.
Besides Dabolim, three centres recorded moderate rainfall during the 24 hours till Saturday morning. Mormugao received 30.6mm, Panaji 19.2mm and Ponda 10.2mm. Four other centres recorded very light rainfall: Mapusa (2.3mm), Sanguem (1.7mm), Old Goa (1.1mm) and Sankhali (0.2mm). The state recorded an average of 14.1mm.
In the 24 hours till Friday morning, only Canacona and Mormugao had recorded rainfall, at 4.2mm and 1mm, respectively.
At this stage of the post-monsoon season, Goa should have received 109.6mm of rainfall.
However, the cumulative total stood at just 17.5mm till Saturday morning.
Goa had been experiencing hot and humid conditions for nearly a week, with the maximum temperature rising above 36°C since Sunday. The India Meteorological Department (IMD), Panaji, recorded a maximum temperature of 37.2°C, the highest in nearly 20 years.
The rainfall deficit stood at 84.1% over the weekend, with El Nino conditions expected to significantly influence weather patterns from Oct to Feb 2027. “Its global effect will be felt all over the Indian subcontinent, including Goa,” said M R Ramesh Kumar, retired chief scientist at the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) and a meteorologist.
The northeast monsoon has already set in over southeast peninsular India. “But Goa does not come under its influence or retreating monsoon,” Kumar said.
IMD, Panaji, has forecast thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds of 30-40kmph at isolated places till Sunday, followed by light rain over the next four days.

Extreme heat pushed English vineyards to harvest grapes up to a month early
The accelerated 2026 ripening raised fears that lower acidity could complicate sparkling production and alter a hallmark style
Saturday, October 17, 2026
English winemakers are bringing in grapes weeks earlier than usual this year after one of the hottest and driest summers on record accelerated ripening and forced producers to reconsider one of the category’s defining traits: high natural acidity.
Across southern England, some vineyards began harvesting in late August and early September, and others were already making urgent decisions about picking dates by the first week of September, according to producers and industry figures cited by 67 Pall Mall. WineGB, the trade body for the English wine industry, took the unusual step of seeking permission for producers to acidify their wines, reflecting concern that the 2026 growing season could leave grapes with less freshness than English wine is known for.
That issue matters most for sparkling wine, which has driven much of England’s rise in recent years. Warmer weather can help still wines by increasing ripeness and flavor, but it can create problems for sparkling producers if sugars rise too far and potential alcohol climbs too high in base wines. Emma Rice, a consultant winemaker and former head winemaker at Hampshire producer Hattingley Valley, told 67 Pall Mall that once the potential alcohol of a base wine moves above 12%, the second fermentation in bottle can become difficult.
The result was an unfamiliar problem in a country where growers have long worried more about grapes failing to ripen than ripening too fast. Rice said some producers left fruit hanging too long and risked losing the option to make sparkling wine unless they blended with lower-alcohol reserve wines from earlier years. She described the need to think about acidification, and to worry about overripe fruit in early September, as something the industry had not faced before.
In many years, English growers wait as long as possible before harvesting, often pushed into picking by rain, disease pressure or falling leaves. This season, growers had to watch sugar levels closely and make active choices much earlier. Grapes in some parts of the country were picked as much as a month ahead of normal schedules, according to the report.
At Gusbourne in Kent, harvesting started on Aug. 26 and ended on Sept. 18, about two weeks earlier than in 2025. The producer described the vintage as an “exceptional” year with ripe and concentrated fruit. Head winemaker Mary Bridges told 67 Pall Mall she was especially encouraged by the quality of Pinot Noir, saying the fruit was clean, evenly ripened and concentrated. She said the still Pinot Noir looked so strong that the winery faced the unusual question of whether it could make enough of it without diverting fruit from sparkling production.
Other producers also reported benefits, especially in still wines. Ruth Simpson of Simpsons Wine Estate in Kent, where still wines account for about two-thirds of production, said the season had brought lower disease pressure and stronger natural sugar development, producing riper and more concentrated fruit. She said that was particularly helpful for a producer focused heavily on still wines because it reduced the need for green harvesting, yield control and weed control.
Rice said she has noticed a broader shift in the last couple of years as more English producers give still wines greater attention. Fruit that she would usually assess at the end of October or even in November was ready for review at the end of September this year. She said Pinot Noir remains difficult for top-level red wines in England, but the variety is capable of producing very good rosés under the right conditions.
For producers buying fruit rather than growing it themselves, the season has also created an unusual opportunity. Sergio Verrillo, co-founder and winemaker at London urban winery Blackbook, said 2026 could be an exceptional year, particularly for still wines, because of the combination of quality, ripeness and concentration in the fruit. At the same time, he said the season could not be discussed without acknowledging climate change, which is giving growers more flexibility in ripening fruit while also forcing them to adapt their vineyard and winery practices.
Not every producer responded by picking early. Domaine Evremond, the Kent venture backed by Champagne Taittinger, started harvesting in mid-September and brought in its last Pinot on Sept. 25. Christelle Rinville, Taittinger’s vineyard director, told 67 Pall Mall that flexibility was essential and that decisions had to depend on vine profile, house style and whether a producer wanted to manage aromatics through sugar or acidity. Rinville, who oversaw the English harvest after finishing in Champagne, said the 2026 season was the first clear example she had seen of climate change having a major effect on the English harvest.
She said the growing season has shortened sharply over time. Two or three decades ago, she said, there were about 100 days between flowering and harvest in England. Over the past 10 years, that interval had dropped to around 85 days, and now it is closer to 75.
The English experience is part of a wider European pattern this year. Harvests have also come early in France, Spain and Italy, with hot conditions and lower yields creating pressure across major wine regions. According to the 67 Pall Mall report, France’s Agriculture Ministry forecast the country’s lowest production in 70 years, while Bordeaux authorities approved emergency irrigation despite the region’s traditionally strict stance against watering vineyards.
That wider context is important for beverage companies and buyers because it shows that higher temperatures do not simply benefit cooler wine regions. In England, a warmer season may improve still wines and help some producers ripen fruit more consistently, but it can also change the profile of sparkling wines, alter alcohol and acidity levels, reduce yields and force faster decisions in vineyards and cellars. For merchants, restaurants and retailers that depend on English sparkling wine’s established style, those changes could affect blend choices, release profiles and supply planning from one vintage to the next.
Even so, producers are not treating 2026 as a settled turning point. Simpson said she had also been concerned by very dry conditions and the threat of water stress, which can cut yields. With a global surplus of wine still weighing on the market, some producers see lower volumes and higher quality as manageable in the short term, but they are also watching whether extreme heat becomes more common.
Bridges warned against assuming that one hot year defines a new pattern. She noted that only two years ago English producers dealt with an exceptionally wet and difficult season. In her view, strong vintage variation remains a basic feature of English wine.

It’s official: Richmond’s new mayor is Rob Howard.
“The work begins tomorrow,” he said on Saturday night following the vote count.
Howard grew emotional as he accepted the results.
“I am deeply honoured that the people of Richmond have placed their trust in me,” he said. “I promise to work every day to maintain that trust.”
Howard was elected with 19,676 votes. Alexa Loo of Richmond Strong had 18,796 votes, while Kash Heed received 11,111 votes.
Howard called it a night of mixed emotions — none of the five council candidates on his Richmond Forward team were elected.
“To the newly elected members of council, regardless of affiliation, I extend my hand in co-operation,” he said.
Howard pledged his commitment to responsible spending, safer streets and “a more vibrant Richmond.”
Howard’s slim lead in Richmond fluctuated with every new voting place reporting, but held throughout the evening.
Supporters at Lavash Seafood Grill on Steveston’s waterfront exploded into cheers before the final results were in, but Howard maintained a sensible guarded optimism even as his team celebrated.
“I knew it would be close,” he said.
Loo called to concede, and shortly afterward came to shake Howard’s hand.
“It was the closest race in B.C., so congratulations to Rob,” she said.
Loo said she appreciated all the support from Richmond voters, and is looking forward to going on vacation.
Heed was not available for comment.
Howard said endorsements from outgoing mayor Malcolm Brodie, who was on-site as returns came in, and former mayor Greg Halsey-Brandt, gave his team a bump.
“They made a big difference,” he said.
Brodie declined to comment, saying only that, “This is Rob’s night.”
Councillors elected were Gary Law, Carol Day, Michael Wolfe, Sheldon Starrett, Laura Gillanders, Kenny Chiu, Kevin Lai and Andy Hobbs.
Richmond Forward council candidates Romeo Bicego, Howard Jampolsky, Melissa Zhang, Eric Yung and Shelley Leonhardt were not elected.
School trustees elected are: Ken Hamaguchi, Heather Larson, Rod Belleza, Danny Chang, Dean Billings, Alice Wong and Donna Sargent.
Richmond voters were still trickling into polling stations just minutes before they closed on Saturday night, after a record 17,464 people voted in the five advance voting days earlier this month, nearly double the advance voters in the past municipal election. The turnout in Richmond’s last election was just 16 per cent, the lowest of all Metro regions in 2022.
Howard was a Richmond councillor from 2001 to 2008, and was elected as MLA for Richmond Centre in 2009 with the B.C. Liberals.
As voting unfolded, Heed campaign director Kal Mahal was tracking his candidate’s voters, in a kind of straw poll as he had shared his cellphone number with decided Heed voters, and asked them to share photographs of their marked ballots. But the mood remained quiet at Heed’s viewing party when early results showed the race was focused on Howard and Loo.
During the campaign, Richmond candidates outlined plans on handling divisive issues such as supervised consumption sites, cost of living, public safety, private property rights and affordable housing in a district that saw homelessness almost double between 2020 and 2025.
Howard and Richmond Forward ran on a family-values campaign that included a ban on supervised injection sites in Richmond and safety audits within 800 metres of schools, a freeze on public development permit application fees, defined service targets, a review of city spending, and fast-tracked seniors housing.
Howard laid out a vision for an expanded arts, culture and entertainment district at the City Centre Waterfront, as well as the development of a trade and exhibition centre for Richmond.
Under the Richmond Strong banner, Loo put safety first, promising to create a community team to respond to public disorder, problem spots and encampments. She promised more fiscal accountability and transparency, including a line-by-line review of municipal spending.
Loo promised faster turnaround on business licensing and building approvals, with infrastructure growth tied to development. She also promised to beef up dike and flood protection, and affordable housing for seniors.
Heed ran as an independent, declaring his opposition to supervised consumption sites and a commitment to law and order. He also promised to cut “red tape” in the development permitting process by reducing wait-times, a predictable property tax strategy with major capital projects subject to referendums and the development of strategic investment opportunities to boost Richmond’s economy.
He also planned to ensure greater transparency in council decision-making and term limits for councillors.

BERHAMPUR: The Ganjam district administration has completed the assessment of damage caused by the 2026 deep depression-induced floods and disbursed the entire amount received from the state relief commissioner (SRC) under specified relief and response heads to local authorities for relief and recovery measures.
The total allocation and additional releases amounted to more than Rs 6.61 crore. According to a district administration release, the deep depression affected an estimated 56,000 people across 22 blocks, 42 gram panchayats, 56 villages and five urban local bodies.
The assessment of damage to houses and other private property, along with agricultural losses, has been completed. Around 4,200 hectares of crop area were affected, of which 3,402.33 hectares suffered crop damage exceeding 33 per cent. The estimated agricultural loss stood at Rs 5.41 crore. The disaster also resulted in the loss of around 10,700 poultry birds.
In the first phase, Rs 2 crore was made available for relief and recovery activities. Of this, Rs 63 lakh was earmarked for relief materials and related assistance, Rs 48 lakh for house-building assistance and Rs 89 lakh for agricultural input subsidy. In the subsequent phase, the SRC released more than Rs 4.52 crore towards agricultural input subsidy and over Rs 8 lakh for search-and-rescue operations.
The administration said the amount received had been disbursed to facilitate agricultural assistance, house-building support, relief distribution and emergency response measures in accordance with government norms.
During the emergency, 66 relief camps were opened across the district, providing temporary shelter to 2,428 people. Arrangements were made for accommodation, food, clothing, medical care and other essential items to meet the needs of affected and evacuated families. The expenditure on relief-camp operations stood at more than Rs 23 lakh. This included over Rs 17 lakh for food and more than Rs 4.5 lakh for other essential items.
The administration clarified that the expenditure on relief camps was separate from the total funds received from the SRC.

Heavy rains pound Chennai as monsoon enters active phase; yellow alert in 17 districts
Heavy overnight showers inundated parts of Chennai, disrupting traffic, as Uthiramerur recorded 15 cm of rainfall
Chennai, Oct 18 (PTI) Heavy rains lashed Chennai and its neighbouring districts, marking the first spell of the northeast monsoon, the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) said here on Sunday.
Several parts of the city witnessed cloudbursts on Saturday night, leaving many localities inundated and causing traffic disruptions.
North Chennai bore the initial brunt, recording between 6 cm and 10 cm of rainfall in less than an hour.
Uthiramerur in Kancheepuram district received the maximum rainfall of 15 cm during the last 24 hours, ending at 5.30 pm on Saturday, followed by a 12 cm downpour at Manalurpet in Kallakurichi during the same period.
The RMC and the India Meteorological Department (IMD) confirmed that the northeast monsoon has entered an active phase.
The deluge was driven by an upper-air cyclonic circulation over north Tamil Nadu and coastal Andhra Pradesh, alongside a trough extending from Lakshadweep to the southwest Bay of Bengal.
The IMD has issued a yellow alert for 17 districts, including Chennai, Tiruvallur, Chengalpattu, Kancheepuram, Cuddalore, and Tiruchi, until October 23.
A yellow alert means heavy rainfall between 6 cm and 11 cm.
Meteorologists forecast that widespread rainfall will continue across several districts -- Chennai, Chengalpattu, Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram, Villupuram, Cuddalore, Mayiladuthurai, Nagapattinam, Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Pudukkottai, Ramanathapuram, Sivaganga, Thoothukudi, Kallakurichi, Ariyalur, Perambalur, Tiruchirappalli, Nilgiris, Coimbatore and Tirunelveli.
Rains are also expected in Puducherry and Karaikal, it said. PTI

Fires in Indonesia that have sent toxic smoke disrupting daily life across South-East Asia has triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc’s meteorological monitor.
The months-long pollution spell has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Timor-Leste.
The Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said in a notice on its website on Friday that it had activated “Alert Level 3 for the Southern Asean region” – the highest rung of a four-tiered alert system.
The alert level is triggered when there is a “high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region” and is reserved for widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days.
The ASMC has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year, according to its website.
Singapore ranked second on IQAir’s live ranking of the world’s most polluted major cities behind Baghdad yesterday, with Kuala Lumpur third. All readings showed “very hazardous” levels”.
Indonesia said yesterday it had been using dry ice at one of South Sumatra province’s main airports in an attempt to disperse the haze.
The country’s national disaster mitigation agency said that 2.4 tonnes of dry ice were dispersed by plane.
The haze has sparked fresh calls for action from residents in Kuala Lumpur.
“It’s a bit unfair on Malaysia because of the irresponsible behaviour of our neighbouring country,” Khairul Azhar, a 33-year-old bank officer said.
“This is affecting our weekend routine – not just for us but many Malaysians,” he said.
In Timor-Leste, unhealthy air pollution persisted yesterday, including in the capital Dili, according to IQAir.
Authorities warned that the situation may worsen and schools were closed.
Singapore said Friday it would issue warnings to seven companies in Indonesia it identified as responsible for the fires.
The companies named by the Singaporean government are mainly pulpwood and timber suppliers in Sumatra and include Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau and SBA Wood Industries.
Philippines foreign department spokesman for Asean issues, Dominic Xavier Imperial, said Friday that the haze would be discussed at upcoming meetings ahead of a November Asean summit in Manila. — AFP
